@@132679977 <p> On May 29 , 2014 , some 30,000 guests streamed through the university 's wrought-iron gates and into Harvard Yard , settling into rows of folding chairs . The sound of church bells floated through the air , and the pageantry of the 363rd commencement unfolded in ritual calm . <p> " Mr. Sheriff , pray give us order ! " said the university marshal , in accordance with tradition . The sheriff of Middlesex County , wearing a silk top hat , banged a cane on the stage three times . " The meeting will be in order ! " <p> Harvard did n't have just any singer perform " The Star-Spangled Banner " that day , it had Aretha Franklin , the queen of soul herself . Michael Bloomberg , the billionaire former mayor of New York City , had prepared a keynote speech . Alan Garber , Harvard 's provost at the time , would award an honorary doctorate to 89-year-old George H.W. Bush , the former Republican president . <p> Amid the sea of caps and gowns , the faces of the Class of 2014 told a story of transformation . An institution once reserved exclusively for the sons of New England 's Brahmin elite was sending off one of its most diverse classes ever . Women made up 47 percent of the more than 1,600 seniors ; 54 percent of the graduates were Black , Latino , Asian-American , multiracial , or hailed from abroad . <p> University leaders prized the school'sdiversity -- not least president Drew Faust , Harvard 's first female president . It was a sign they were training the next generation of global leaders . <p> By some measures , Harvard had already cornered that market . The university had produced 160 Nobel Prize laureates , over 100 billionaires , and eight US presidents -- Harvard Law grad Barack Obama was then well into his second term . <p> " We were the generation of hope , " recalled Yolanda Borquaye , who led the Association of Black Harvard Women and graduated that day . <p> A special commencement program celebrated Harvard scholars making breakthroughs in science and medicine , leading in education and the arts , and fighting poverty . Donations from across the political spectrum were pouring in from alumni , including multimillion dollar gifts from two billionaire hedge fund managers , Bill Ackman of New York and Ken Griffin of Chicago . The university was running nearly 900 research projects around the world . <p> " Harvard is making a difference now , " the program said , " and is working to lead the way in the next decade . " <p> Few at the 2014 commencement could have predicted that , a decade later , President Trump would target Harvard with the most severe set ofsanctions ever imposed on a major university , casting it and other elite institutions as radical forces undermining America . Fewer still could have anticipated how Harvard 's confrontation with Trump would reflect the nation 's own conflicts over who we are and what we want to stand for . <p> One person at commencement did see ominous warnings , however : Bloomberg , who was raised nearby in working-class Medford . That afternoon , he stepped to the podium to deliver a somewhat unusual speech for a happy occasion . " There is no easy time to say hard things , " he said . <p> Bloomberg had been observing escalating rancor in Congress and the political undermining of science and research expertise . On college campuses , there were other worrying trends : invitations to conservative speakers rescinded after student protests , the shaming of professors whose views violated progressive norms , and colleges becoming liberal echo chambers . <p> " Think about the irony , " Bloomberg said . " In the 1950s , the right wing was attempting to repress left-wing ideas . Today , on many college campuses , it is liberals trying to repress conservative ideas , even as conservative faculty members are at risk of becoming an endangered species . " <p> Bloomberg challenged students to fight the urge to shout down people with different views . Higher education is " perpetually vulnerable to the tyrannical tendencies of monarchs , mobs , and majorities , " he warned . <p> And the winds of politics have a way of shifting quickly . <p> Aretha Franklin , Michael Bloomberg , and George H.W. Bush at the 2014 Harvard commencement , where they all received honorary degrees . ( Lane Turner/Globe Staff ) <p> Bloomberg 's speech might have been more prophetic than even he intended . <p> Five months later , the US midterm elections delivered a historic red wave . Republicans regained control of the Senate and strengthened their House majority to a level not seen in nearly a century . Among the House freshmen was 30-year-old Elise Stefanik , a Harvard alumna and , at the time , the youngest woman ever elected to Congress . In a decade , she 'd help lead a battle against the college that educated her . <p> Then there was Donald Trump . <p> Two days before Harvard 's 2014 commencement , the real estate magnate and reality show star was the featured guest at the National Press Club luncheon , not far from the White House . <p> He had been watching the Tea Party gaining strength , calling for a political reckoning in Washington . In his speech , he lingered on some of his favorite themes . Obama 's birth certificate . His talent for building brands and crushing foes on Twitter . How America 's economy was a loser compared to China . <p> " It 's about winning , " Trump said , no fewer than seven times in his talk . <p> Trump was asked why he had n't run for president . " If I do n't see the right person I will do something in ' 16 , " he vowed . " I will do it as sure as you 're sitting here . " <h> Why Harvard ? <p> How the world 's most powerful university found itself under brutal attack by the world 's most powerful man will be debated for years . <p> Was President Trump 's decisionto freeze more than$2 billion of Harvard 's federal research funding , threaten its ability to bring in foreign students , and impose a slew of other sanctions just a power play ? A media-obsessed president relishing the spectacle of going after the nation 's most famous college ? <p> But for others , that explanation overlooks a deeper reality . When Trump turned his fire on Harvard , vast swaths of the country went along . Many Americans even cheered . <p> How did Harvard find itself in this position ? Since the summer , Globe reporters have studied this question , poring over legal filings , research reports , and campus surveys , and speaking with more than 150 people , including Harvard administrators , faculty , alumni , students , higher-education leaders , and public officials . Many declined to be named because of ongoing negotiations between Harvard and the White House . <p> There are no simple answers , only a collage of overlapping narratives that shared one theme : Over the past decade , as political and cultural upheavals fractured the nation , and social media intensified every divide , Harvard became the university that plenty of everyday Americans loved to hate . <p> Trump was determined to attack the elites , and Harvard had a bullseye on its back . ( Video : Randy Vazquez/Globe staff , Photo : Jessica Rinaldi/Globe staff ) <p> Harvard 's leaders say they have strived to be on the right side of history , guided by the school 's motto " Veritas , " the Latin word for truth . They embraced the values of multiculturalism and international engagement as integral to a 21st century education . Students and faculty who leaned into this decade 's major social movements -- such as Black Lives Matter , MeToo , LGBTQ rights -- were seen as positively engaging with the nation and the world . <p> But during this period , Harvard paid less attention to other issues , including a growing intolerance on campus for any views that might seem to challenge its egalitarian mission . Students and professors alike became increasingly afraid of speaking their minds , especially if their ideas clashed with the progressive ethos . By 2024 , Harvard found two out of three graduating seniors feared sharing their beliefs about controversial subjects in class . <p> While Harvard was embracing the ideals of racial justice and global involvement over this decade , many Americans outside the university 's ivy-clad walls were turning away from those values . Or perhaps had never supported them in the first place . A conservative narrative rose that Harvard was full of itself and worse , in ways undermining what was best for America . <p> Lawrence Bacow bristles at that notion . During his Harvard presidency , between 2018 and 2023 , he helped commission military cadets in the ROTC program . " I would remind them that Harvard was 140 years old when the Declaration of Independence was signed , " Bacow recalled . Eight Harvard alumni signed it , and five were framers of the US Constitution . <p> Advertisement <p> " My point was that Harvard literally helped to bring this country into being , " he told the Globe . " So this notion that we do n't care about our country -- it 's just , as you can tell , it gets my blood boiling . " <p> The crisis of trust in higher education extended well beyond Harvard . From 2015 to 2023 , the percentage of Americans who expressed high confidence in colleges and universities collapsed from 57 percent to 36 percent , according to Gallup . But the nation 's most famous university was bound to attract the bulk of the negative attention . <p> From 2014 to 2025 , Harvard coverage on Fox News far surpassed any other top 20 university in the US News &amp; World Report rankings , according to a Globe review . Harvard was the subject of more than 300 stories -- nearly twice as many as Columbia University , the second most covered -- and almost all of them framed as examples of liberal excess . <p> Higher education 's costs were also soaring , and Harvard , with its $57 billion endowment , was the gilded example : Though it offers generous financial aid packages , Harvard charges $87,000 a year for its undergraduate education . That sticker price is bigger than the median annual household income in the US . And the college , which rejected 96 percent of its 50,000 or so applicants this year , continues to give admission boosts to children of alumni , known as legacies . <p> Could Harvard have done anything to dodge the worst of Trump 's attacks ? Many would say absolutely not -- he was always going to go after the biggest brand in college . But others saw how vulnerabilities developed over years made the university a perfect target for a president like Trump . <p> Rakesh Khurana was dean of Harvard College from 2014 through this past summer , and central to many of Harvard 's efforts to bridge divides over race , class , and politics . A sociologist by training , he now teaches at the college and Harvard Business School . <p> Professor Rakesh Khurana , shown at Harvard Business School , served as dean of Harvard College from 2014 through this summer . ( Craig F. Walker/Globe Staff ) <p> In interviews this fall , he paused when asked how Harvard found itself in this crisis with Trump . There are no simple answers , he said , but he offered an analogy : the fires that swept through Los Angeles earlier this year . <p> " Everybody 's like : ' Was it a match ? ' ' Was it a lightning strike ? ' " Khurana said . But what sparked the fires is only part of the story ; the other part is what allowed the flames to spread . " You also have all these houses built up close , " he said . " You have climate change , so it 's so dry now . You have the Santa Ana winds . You have buildings that are not up to code . " <p> " Until you take care of the conditions that set you up for that awful event , " Khurana said , " it 's going to happen again . " <p> Trump lit the match at Harvard , there 's no doubt about that . But before he did , the university 's leaders knew they had conditions on campus that needed to change . <h> Viral moments <p> In the spring of 2016 , as trees sprouted leaves outside her office in Harvard Yard , Faust was about to enter her 10th year as president . She was contemplating when to step down , yet still wrestling with a troubling piece of unfinished business : how to ensure students of all backgrounds felt supported by the university . <p> Faust had lived through tumultuous periods of change in her own life . A civil rights champion raised in the segregated South , she was deeply committed to the pluralistic ideal of America . She saw that bringing a broad range of students to Cambridge -- people of different races and religions , of different economic backgrounds , from different countries -- forged better ideas and a stronger education for everyone . <p> This environment produced robust debate and sometimes led to participation in the school 's history of campus activism , including large-scale protests against the Vietnam War , South Africa 's apartheid regime , and America 's income inequality . <p> " Out of that unruliness comes the odd idea that may change the world , " Faust said . <h> A changing Harvard campus <p> In 2016 , the campus was the most racially and ethnically diverse it had ever been . Because the size of Harvard 's undergraduate class had stayed the same for decades , white students made up a smaller proportion : 41 percent of Harvard 's American undergrads identified as white that year , roughly half of the percentage in 1980 , according to government data . <p> The decrease in white students produced other demographic shifts . About 10 percent of Harvard undergraduates were Jewish in 2016 , down from roughly 20 to 25 percent in the 1980s , student surveys show . The population of Muslims , Hindus , and Buddhists was growing , but still small -- about 5 percent collectively . <p> Harvard leaders could tell the air between students sometimes felt charged . " These differences could create stresses and tensions , " Faust recalled . " There were outcomes we had , in some cases , not fully anticipated . " <p> In 2012 , for example , 20-year-old junior Sarah Siskind touched off a campus controversy by publishing an op-ed in the Harvard Crimson , the student newspaper , that criticized affirmative action admissions policies based on race . Siskind , a libertarian , started out light -- joking there was no special boost for other disadvantaged groups like short or dumb people -- and then got more serious . <p> Siskind was concerned about the drawbacks of giving certain groups special advantages . She admitted she was a legacy applicant and worried she 'd taken a spot from a more deserving student . And she suggested all students admitted under more lenient standards might be regarded with " greater skepticism " by future employers . " Racism persists , despite over a century of incredible progress , " she wrote , " but affirmative action imbeds racism in the lives of future generations . " <p> To some students of color , the column was a personal affront , denying how amply qualified they were at a school that relied on multiple criteria for admission . <p> In a response published in the Crimson , Borquaye and two other leaders of Black student groups also explained how racism was inescapable for them no matter where they went . " Minorities can expect to experience racially prejudiced interactions in almost every part of their daily lives , regardless of their elevated socio-economic or educational statuses , " they wrote . <p> Sarah Siskind , a 2014 graduate of Harvard College , with her senior thesis adviser , Prof. Harvey Mansfield . Photo taken while she was an undergraduate . <p> In May 2014 , Yolanda Borquaye , a graduating senior from Georgia , spoke at a special commencement event at Cabot House at Harvard . <p> The dispute spread across campus , but not beyond . Social media in 2012was still mostly used by people to post birthday photos or bond over shared interests . " I would definitely have been canceled if it happened now , " Siskind said recently . <p> Now a science and comedy writer in New York City , she does n't regret publishing the column , but she wishes she could rewrite it to more fully recognize inequalities in educational opportunities . " I would be less flippant , " she said . <p> Some Harvard faculty turned the campus controversy into a teaching moment , organizing discussion forums that included the two women , who ended up on friendly terms as a result . It felt like there were more opportunities for productive " consciousness raising " in those days , said Borquaye , now a lawyer in London . <p> " We had more civil discourse then because it was more often in person , " she said . " I feel a bit of nostalgia for that time because we were n't all glued to our phones . " <p> That was changing rapidly , for better and worse . By 2014 , Americans had passed an important threshold : More young adults owned smartphones than computers , research shows , and social media use was soaring . <p> A new generation of students was " more willing than earlier generations to speak up about their perceived areas of injustice or unfairness , " said Khurana , the former undergraduate dean . Social media allowed them to express ways their classmates or universities made them feel like outsiders -- to raise awareness and demand better in a wider way . <p> In the spring of 2014 , a multimedia project called " I , Too , Am Harvard " showed up first on Tumblr , and then went viral after being picked up by BuzzFeed and other news sites . <p> Carol Powell/Tumblr <p> Created by a student , Kimiko Matsuda-Lawrence , the project included dozens of Black students holding placards that responded to hurtful comments they 'd heard at Harvard . <p> " Having an opinion does not make me an ' Angry Black Woman ' " read one . <p> Another student held a card that included the comment " I do n't see COLOR , " and asked " Does that mean you do n't see Me ? " <p> The project spread rapidly to other schools in the US -- " I , Too , Am NYU , " and " I , Too , Am Princeton " -- as well as universities in Canada and England . <p> Just a few months later , the power of social media was fully revealed . After the August 2014 police shooting of 18-year-old Michael Brown in Ferguson , Mo. , bystanders ' photos of his body posted on social media helped spread the Black Lives Matter movement nationwide . <p> Two opposing forces -- support for racial equality and a backlash to it -- emerged simultaneously , including on the Harvard campus . In 2015 , students organized a campaign to change the law school 's crest , which was linked to an 18th century family of slave owners who funded the school . Amid that call , vandals defaced framed portraits of Black faculty by placing black tape over their faces . <p> A 2014 " die-in " protest at Harvard Medical School , in response to the decision by authorities to not bring indictments in the police killings of Michael Brown in Ferguson , Mo. , and Eric Garner in New York . ( David L. Ryan/Globe Staff ) <p> " This is my portrait at Harvard Law School , " wrote Ronald Sullivan Jr . on Twitter , sending out a photo . He was one of 12 permanent full-time Black faculty at the school , out of 125 . The acts of vandalism were investigated as a hate crime and spurred the racial reckoning at the law school , which led to the crest being replaced . <p> As the 2015-16 academic year came to a close , it was clear to Harvard 's leaders that they still had important work to do to improve campus culture . Faust established a Presidential Task Force on Inclusion and Belonging , pulling together more than 50 faculty , staff , students , and alumni to work on solutions not just at the college , but at all of the many graduate and professional schools . <p> Danielle Allen , a professor of political philosophy , co-chaired the task force . Raised in a family with a prominent Black conservative father , she wanted it to address the needs of the university 's demographic groups , but also to go further . It should engage with the fact that politically conservative and religious students could feel marginalized on campus . <p> Allen reached out to a member of Harvard 's Republican student committee , Kent Haeffner , a varsity swimmer and a devout Christian . He 'd caught her attention by publicly criticizing the task force 's early decision to drop a reference to the Puritans from the school song , " Fair Harvard . " The university was founded in 1636 . Erasing its religious origins seemed absurd to Haeffner . <p> When they met in person , Haeffner said he was n't afraid to speak his mind , even on a campus dominated by liberal students . This was just the kind of perspective Allen knew Harvard needed . <h> Pranking Trump <p> The perception that the Harvard community was overwhelmingly liberal was not an exaggeration . <p> In 2016 , about 68 percent of the graduating seniors identified as " liberal " or " very liberal , " according to a survey by the Crimson , while just 8 percent said they were conservative or very conservative . Political moderates made up 22 percent , and 2 percent of respondents said they were apolitical . <p> There were signs the balance was even further tilted away from conservatives among faculty , instructors , and researchers . Between 2011 and 2014 , a separate Crimson analysis found , 84 percent of federal contributions from those groups went to Democratic campaigns and political action committees . The number rose to 96 percent among people affiliated with the faculty of Arts and Sciences . <p> After Trump announced his presidential bid in June 2015 , plenty of people at Harvard found the idea of him winning unimaginable . The student Republican club later withheld its endorsement of Trump , declining to support a GOP candidate for the first time since 1888 . " The rhetoric he espouses -- from racist slander to misogynistic taunts -- is not consistent with our conservative principles , " the group said . <p> Others at Harvard showed their disbelief in a different way , pulling off an epic prank . <p> In the summer of 2015 , writers for the Lampoon , the student humor publication , reached out to Trump 's campaign posing as Crimson staff . Tom Waddick , then 20 , said they 'd like to come to Manhattan and snap a photo of Trump sitting in the Crimson president 's special , throne-like chair , to go with an endorsement of him for president . The campaign agreed . <p> On the appointed day , Lampoon members hauled the chair -- temporarily liberated from the Crimson 's office -- into Trump Tower in Manhattan . Trump turned on the charm , saying they could touch his hair if they wanted to prove it was real . If they wanted him to speak at Harvard , he said , he 'd waive his hefty fee -- that was " a very good deal , " he noted . <p> " It was like he was there to entertain us , " recalled Waddick , now 31 , who grew up in Waltham and is presently a writer in Los Angeles . With unwitting campaign staff looking on , everyone posed for the picture giving Trump 's signature thumbs up . <p> Members of the Harvard Lampoon traveled to Trump Tower to pose with presidential candidate Donald Trump . They 'd convinced his campaign they were from the Harvard student newspaper , which they said would endorse him . Todd Waddick was standing at the immediate left of the chair , over Trump 's right shoulder . <p> Soon after the fake endorsement went up on a fake Crimson webpage , Waddick 's cellphone rang . It was Michael Cohen , Trump 's lawyer , yelling . He threatened to come to Cambridge himself , to make sure every student involved was expelled . <p> Looking back , Waddick said he got a preview of the future Trump administration 's bullying tactics . " Sad to say , it often works , " he said . The Lampoon agreed to take the site down . <p> Trump did n't say anything publicly about the prank , though spokesperson Hope Hicks issued a statement . " The students who perpetrated this are fraudsters and liars , but frankly it was a waste of only a few minutes , " it said . " Mr. Trump attended the great Wharton School of Finance , a school that has more important things to do . " <p> Trump also had more important things to do , like winning a presidential election . <p> At packed political rallies in oft-overlooked parts of the country , he tapped into authentic populist anger , speaking out against global trade agreements and championing issues embraced by evangelical Christians . With the help of political strategist Steve Bannon , he also leaned into anti-immigration messages , including his vows to ban Muslims and build a border wall to keep out Mexicans . <p> The morning after Trump 's victory , students in Harvard Yard moved in slow motion -- dazed , disbelieving , and , in many cases , devastated . <p> " I feel like it 's a nightmare that just came true , " one told the Crimson . <p> In his role as dean , Khurana typed an email to undergraduates . He tried to speak to all of them , whatever their political leanings . " In spite of our differences , " he wrote , " we can only move forward as friends , neighbors , and classmates if we develop the capacity to understand and empathize with each other . " <p> It was a hopeful message , but aspirational language could only do so much to bring people together . <p> " We were trying to do something difficult , " Khurana said this fall . " Something that the country has n't figured out . " <h> Defining diversity <p> On campus , Harvard 's leaders remained fully committed to diversifying their student body , including by expanding access across socio-economic lines . They believed these students should also feel they belonged on a campus where plenty of classmates had trust funds and vacation homes . <p> Harvard students held signs before a rally in January of 2017 , which included asking the university to protect undocumented students and Muslim students . ( Jessica Rinaldi/Globe Staff ) <p> By this time , roughly 15 percent of Harvardundergraduates were the first in their families to go to college , and more than half received full or partial financial aid . ( Today , Harvard reports that roughly one in four attend for free based on financial eligibility . ) <p> In some quarters , Harvard 's all-male final clubs were seen as perpetuating a culture of exclusivity that needed addressing . The private social societies , some dating back to the 1800s and housed in historic buildings around campus , enjoyed generations of alumni support . They also brought instant connections to elite careers in finance , tech , and consulting that are perennially popular among Harvard students . <p> Starting in 2017 , Harvard administrators , led by president Faust and Khurana , pressed the clubs to admit women . The sanctions they imposed were strict : Members would be barred from captaining universitysports teams and receiving endorsements for fellowships . <p> To Khurana , it seemed like a common sense decision . To others , the university was overreaching . One of Khurana 's predecessors as dean , Harry R. Lewis , urged him to pull back . " The College responds to improper acts , not memberships , " Lewis wrote him in a private letter . <p> The final clubs ultimately prevailed in getting the administration to rescind its sanctions , after a legal ruling in a similar matter hurt Harvard 's position . Still , some donors and alumni felt troubled by what they saw as the university passing sweeping moral judgment on the clubs . <p> The scene at the Fly Club , one of the all-male final clubs at Harvard , on May 7 , 2016 . ( Katherine Taylor/New York Times ) <p> Questions about Harvard 's leadership also surfaced for Ackman , the New York City hedge fund manager and major Harvard donor . The Harvard he remembered so fondly was one of stimulating classes and invigorating crew races on the Charles . But it was now seeming more like an indoctrination factory . <p> Ackman told the Globe his daughter became fascinated with Marxism during her time on campus in the late 2010s . " She came out of Harvard with a very negative view of capitalism generally , " he recalled . " She 'd get incredibly frustrated and upset with me . " <p> He said she began to sympathize with a worldview that largely cast America as a capitalist " oppressor " that victimizes other " oppressed " countries . <p> Today , Ackman said , he believes these kinds of binaries contributed to a campus environment where hateful speech toward groups seen as oppressors could seem justified . <p> " An oppressor-oppressed framework is a framework of resentment , " he said , " where the perception of success is an ill-gotten thing that was only achieved at the expense of someone else . " <p> Around this time , a number of conservative students raised similar concerns . May Mailman , a 2015 law school graduate who would rise quickly in the Trump administration , told the Globe that she saw elite universities including Harvard " glorifying victimization " in a way that stifled free speech and contrary views . <p> But many pushed back on this depiction , saying they are of a generation of minority groups willing to speak up -- and help inform others -- about comments or views that offend . And some have observed that others who demand a blanket right to free speech can use it as a license to say anything they want , no matter how offensive . <p> Noah Harris , a former Harvard student class president who is Black , watched these debates play out during his undergraduate years from 2018 to 2022 . " I do n't believe that every single person who was advocating for free speech at the time had problematic views , " he said . But among them , there were some who used free speech " as almost a shield for problematic ideas . " <p> These challenges came into full view as the politics around Israel sharpened . Several decades ago , the relationship between pro-Israel and pro-Palestinian students at Harvard had been fairly cooperative , including sometimes holding joint programs . But as armed conflicts in the region grew in the 2000s , the relationship between the two groups on campus frayed , according to two major task force reports Harvard released in 2025 . One was on combatting antisemitism and anti-Israel bias , and the other on fighting bias against Muslims , Arabs , and Palestinians . <p> In 2017 , the Palestine Solidarity Committee , a campus group , helped produce a public art installation called the " Wall of Resistance , " set up outside Harvard 's Science Center . The annual project began as a way to show humanitarian suffering broadly . Over time , it focused more on the plight ofPalestinians , with messages like " Zionism is Racism Settler Colonialism White Supremacy Apartheid . " <p> Some Jewish students , their numbers on campus declining in recent decades , felt their concerns about mounting anti-Israel messages on campus were being downplayed by the university administration , according to the antisemitism report . <p> " Every minority group is allowed to define what they consider to be discrimination , but when Jews deem something antisemitic , people do n't take that seriously , " a Jewish student wrote on the Hillel website . <p> Advertisement <p> Meanwhile , support for the Palestinian cause on campus grew , including fromstudents of Middle Eastern , South Asian , and African heritage , some of whom were moved by parallels to their own families ' experiences with mass displacement or Western imperialism . They were joined by other students criticizing Israel 's actions in the West Bank and the blockade of Gaza . <p> Some of these Harvard community members told the task force on bias against Palestinians that their views were being suppressed on campus , which they attributed to pressure from major donors with pro-Israeli views . " I 've never been told by the university I ca n't speak up . But it 's clear it 's different with Palestine issues , " one faculty member said . " The double standards are disheartening . " <h> ' Unchecked emotion ' <p> The leaders of the Inclusion and Belonging task force had hoped to have a broader impact when it released its final report in March 2018 . In retrospect , Allen , the co-chair , said they " did n't put enough bright arrows at the places where we were trying to drive change . " <p> The document was wide ranging in its recommendations , including bringing in more diverse faculty , building a " culture of mutual respect , " and creating more inclusive signage on campus . It also made a point of including " political outlook " as a type of diversity that Harvard should foster . <p> But Allen said the administration did n't end up taking serious steps toward cultivating viewpoint diversity . Instead , she said , the university 's priorities became influenced by national events , especially the surging Black Lives Matter movement that concentrated attention on racial injustice . <p> Kent Haeffner , in the back row left , with other members of the Harvard Republican Club , at a Jeb Bush town hall event in New Hampshire in September 2015 . ( Kent Haeffner ) <p> Haeffner , the Republican Club president , found participating on the task force a positive and eye-opening experience . But it did n't seem to him that promoting dialogue on campus had been a priority , either . What was really needed , he said , was helping students gain skills to constructively engage with ideas they find off-putting . <p> " It 's not enough just to say : ' Hey , you have free speech , ' " said Haeffner , now a consultant in Chicago . " Harvard 's mission is to train the future citizen leaders of the world . And how are you going to be able to train them if we ca n't get them comfortable being exposed to viewpoints different than their own ? " <p> The inclusion report did not deal with one crucial subject at all : how profoundly social media 's frenetic , polarizing churn was affecting campus interactions . <p> Looking back , Faust told the Globe this year that the most underappreciated cultural force at work during her 11-year presidency was the rise of the iPhone and social media . " And it was happening so inexorably , yet so quietly , we did n't fully notice , " she said . " It 's like boiling the frog . " <p> In 2019 , social media helped fan the flames of a controversy related to Sullivan , the Harvard law professor . He had received support as one of the Black faculty of the law school whose portraits were defaced in 2015 . About four years later , though , he became the target of protest himself , when news ricocheted on social media that he was representing Harvey Weinstein , the Hollywood mogulaccused of raping or sexually harassing dozens of women . Weinstein 's case catalyzed the #MeToo movement . <p> A contingent of students loudly demanded Sullivan step down , not from the law school faculty , but from his position as the residential faculty dean of one of Harvard 's dormitories , a position he 'd held for a decade . They said undergraduate women might now feel uncomfortable bringing concerns to him about sexual assault , a campus problem under heightened scrutiny . <p> Khurana and Claudine Gay , then dean of the faculty of Arts and Sciences , both weighed in , and Sullivan was pushed out of the faculty dean 's role , with administrators citing " climate " issues at the dorm . <p> Sullivan later accused Harvard officials of launching a probe tinged with racial bias -- he and his wife were the first Black residential deans in Harvard 's history . And in an op-ed in The New York Times , he asserted that the administration had " capitulated to protesters . " <p> Harvard Law professor Ronald Sullivan , then representing Harvey Weinstein in his sexual assault case , entered court in New York on April 26 , 2019 . ( Richard Drew/Associated Press ) <p> For years , Harvard 's administrators had been talking about how to handle emotionally charged tensions around identity , the kind that can metastasize on social media . But responding quickly has never been Harvard 's strength , Khurana acknowledged . " Our job is to think slow , " he said . " And that was becoming increasingly incongruent with the world that we were moving into . " <h> Attacking elites <p> There were other signs that the national political winds were becoming less favorable to Harvard . <p> By 2021 , an affirmative action case against Harvard had been winding its way to the Supreme Court for years . Students For Fair Admissions , a nonprofit founded by conservative legal strategist Edward Blum , first filed the landmark lawsuit in 2014 , arguing that Harvard 's affirmative action policy discriminated against Asian-American applicants . <p> Trump 's Justice Department later backed Blum 's case and launched its own investigation . " No American should be denied admission to school because of their race , " then-Attorney General Jeff Sessions said in a 2018 statement . " As a recipient of taxpayer dollars , Harvard has a responsibility to conduct its admissions policy without racial discrimination . " <p> Edward Blum , president of Students for Fair Admissions , in Copley Square in 2018 . The group filed a lawsuit claiming Harvard discriminated in admissions . ( Jessica Rinaldi/Globe Staff ) <p> During the case , the university repeatedly contested the plaintiff 's findings and methodology . The trial judge sided with Harvard in 2019 and so did the appeals court in 2020 . <p> But in 2021 , the case landed at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court , which appeared likely to rule against Harvard . <p> There , on a national stage , lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that Harvard not only gave advantages to underrepresented minorities , but also prioritized some already-privileged groups . <p> Its analysis of undergraduate applicants from the classes of 2014 to 2019 found an overall admission rate of about 6 percent . But when you drilled down into different groups , the odds improved . Harvard admitted nearly 34 percent of legacy applicants , as well as 42 percent of students on a special list generally associated with children of current or prospective donors . About 47 percent of the children of faculty and staff got in . <p> It could all look unfair to those hoping to get into Harvard . The undergraduate class size had stayed fairly static for decades , so admissions was essentially a zero-sum game : Advantages to one group took away from the others . And for many , admission policies like these were just one of the many ways the higher education system -- and the nation 's institutions in general - felt skewed against them . <p> As the case played out in court , there would be other stark reminders of societal divides . The COVID-19 pandemic exposed painful class divisions and the Jan. 6 Capitol riot -- the 2021 siege by Trump supporters claiming election fraud in his loss to Joe Biden -- was a sign of just how deep anger ran . <p> Among Trump 's backers questioning the election results was Representative Stefanik , a former moderate Republican who became a staunch Trump ally . As she perpetuated Trump 's claims of fraud , hundreds of students and alumni called on Harvard to cut its ties with her . The Harvard Institute of Politics , a program encouraging students to pursue public service , removed her from its senior advisory committee . <p> To Stefanik , who had been heavily involved at the institutesince her college days , this was just the latest example of Harvard silencing conservative voices . She blasted the organization for " caving to the woke Far-Left . " <h> Warring words <p> The Jan. 6 riot sounded a warning to the pillars of progressive society that the country was profoundly cleaving over race , class , and politics . Harvard doubled down on its inclusive mission . <p> In May 2017 , Harvard graduates took part in the Black Commencement ceremony , a special event during the graduation festivities . ( Keith Bedford/Globe staff ) <p> Bacow , who succeeded Faust as president in 2018 and long championed diversity efforts , put $5 million into a university-wide project to study Harvard 's ties to slavery . In announcing the initiative in November 2019 , he said Harvard has an obligation to understand the school 's past " from the ways the university benefitted from the Atlantic slave trade to the debates and advocacy for abolition on campus . " <p> Over this period , Harvard also continued to promote its central diversity office , to offer support to students and faculty , and to the units that handle bias complaints at the university 's schools . Academic departments began requiring applicants for faculty positions to submit " diversity statements , " asking them to articulate how they would support equity and inclusion efforts on campus . <p> By the summer of 2021 , another instructor on campus found herself at the center of political controversy . That July on " Fox and Friends , " Carole Hooven , a longtime lecturer in Harvard 's human evolutionary biology department , was asked to respond to news that some in medical schools felt pressure to use trans-inclusive terms , such as " pregnant people " rather than " pregnant women . " <p> Hooven was frustrated by how " ideology has been infiltrating science , " she said on the news show . " The facts are that there are , in fact , two sexes , " she continued . " There are male and female , and those sexes are designated by the kinds of gametes we produce . " <p> However , science and empathy were n't mutually exclusive , Hooven added . " We can treat people with respect and respect their gender identities and use their preferred pronouns , " she said , " so understanding the facts about biology does n't prevent us from treating people with respect . " <p> Fox News <p> The interview outraged Laura Simone Lewis , a graduate student in Hooven 's department and director of its diversity and inclusion task force . She tweeted a clip of Hooven 's TV interview with a message : " I am appalled and frustrated by the transphobic and harmful remarks made by a member of my dept in this interview with Fox and Friends . " <p> Hooven was surprised ; she and Lewis had a cordial relationship . She responded , also on Twitter : " I appreciate your concerns . Could you let me ( and the Twitterverse ) know exactly what I said that you consider transphobic or harmful to undergrads ? I think you know that I care deeply about all of my students , and I also care about science . How about a discussion ? " <p> The Twitter exchange spiraled from there , with others piling on . Hooven had many defenders , but within months , not a single graduate student would agree tohelp teach her course on the role of hormones in behavior , one of the university 's most popular . <p> Hooven had asked top administrators to publicly back her right to speak freely . They never lent her their full support , she said . In early 2023 , she felt her only choice was to leave the job she had loved for two decades . <p> " This is the thing that I can not get over to this day , " Hooven said in an interview with the Globe . " I assumed that the faculty and the administration would have my back . " <p> Hooven 's case was a tipping point for some Harvard faculty concerned about the chilling of speech on campus , an issue some believed was well within Harvard 's control to help fix . They organized the Council on Academic Freedom to promote civil discourse and viewpoint diversity . It drew in some prominent professors who had been outspoken on the issue in the past , such as Steven Pinker of the psychology department , Sullivan of the law school , and Tarek Masoud of the Kennedy School . <p> Masoud told the Globe that students need to know that a robust university education requires feeling some degree of discomfort . He said political analyst Van Jones put it well when he likened college learning to working out at a gym . <p> " Look , this is n't your home . Home is where you feel totally comfortable . You kick off your shoes , you watch too much Netflix , eat some chocolate , " Masoud said . " This is the gym . You 're not going to get stronger at the gym unless you make yourself uncomfortable by doing things like lifting heavy weights . <p> " You 're not going to get anything out of Harvard if you 're always comfortable here . " <p> On July 1 , 2023 , Harvard would get a new president , Claudine Gay , a prominent academic who was hailed for being dedicated to both campus diversity and free speech . " She has a bedrock commitment to free inquiry and expression , as well as a deep appreciation for the diverse voices and views that are the lifeblood of a university community , " said Penny Pritzker , head of the Harvard Corporation , the university 's top governing board . <p> Gay , the daughter of Haitian immigrants , would also be Harvard 's first Black president . And little would be easy about her tenure : Just two days before taking office , the US Supreme Court struck down Harvard 's race-conscious admissions policy . The court 's decision would require changes , she later said , but Harvard 's commitment to diversity " remains steadfast . " <h> The right rises <p> Trump 's movement did not sputter out after he left office in 2021 . The more progressive leaders pushed for their ideals , the harder the right pushed back with a fundamentally different vision of America 's future . <p> As Trump and his allies contemplated their political comeback , they seized on the idea of American cultural decline . Bannon , Trump 's former political strategist and a Harvard Business School graduate , had been fascinated by Hungary , where Prime Minister Viktor Orban set in a motion a series of events to crush liberal universities . <p> " What matters is the survival of the Judeo-Christian West , " Bannon told a crowd in Budapest in 2018 . " The West does not have to decline . This is not a law of physics . It can be reversed . " <p> The conservative activist Christopher Rufo in Tacoma , Wash. , on April 19 , 2022 . ( Chona Kasinger/New York Times ) <p> Another powerful new voice countering the DEI movement was Christopher Rufo , a former filmmaker and conservative writer . He earned a master 's in government at the Harvard Extension School , part of the university 's continuing education department . <p> He seized on a term in scholarly writing , " critical race theory , " and deployed it to describe the work of race-conscious initiatives within corporate HR departments and universities across the country . <p> In the fall of 2021 , an up-and-coming politician focused on higher education at the National Conservatism Conference.JD Vance , a Yale Law-educated Ohio candidate for the US Senate , gave a closing speech titled : " The universities are the enemy . " <p> Vance said universities had become " very hostile institutions " that were pushing DEI mandates , treatments for transgender youth , and training young women to prioritize career over family . <p> " If any of us want to do the things that we want to do for our country , and for the people who live in it , " he said , " we have to honestly and aggressively attack the universities in this country . " <h> October 7th <p> Violet Barron , a sophomore at Harvard , was up late studying in her Adams House dorm room on Oct. 7 , 2023 , when a news alert pinged her phone . Hamas-led militants had stormed into Israeli towns , murdering civilians and taking an untold number of hostages . <p> Barron cried as she scrolled the news online . For comfort in the days to come , she sometimes sang to herself a traditional Hebrew healing prayer , Mi Shebeirach . " I was scared for Israel , " the place whereshehad her Bat Mitzvah , she recalled recently . <p> Ever since Barron was little , growing up outside Los Angeles , she wanted to go to Harvard , just like her father and grandfather . Her first-year experience was similar to her dad 's : great classes and extra-curricular activities and new friends . People did n't always know she was Jewish -- she is biracial , with a Chinese-American mother -- but Judaism from her father 's side meant a lot to her . <p> Barron was among the many people across the political spectrum who were disgusted by a statement posted on Instagram , within hours of the Oct. 7th attack . Signed by the Harvard Undergraduate Palestine Solidarity Committee and more than 30 other campus groups , it blamed Israel for provoking the attack . <p> Instagram <p> " We , the undersigned student organizations , hold the Israeli regime entirely responsible for all unfolding violence , " the statement began . " Today 's events did not occur in a vacuum . For the last two decades , millions of Palestinians in Gaza have been forced to live in an open-air prison . " It went on to warn of a catastrophic counterattack by Israel . <p> The student groups ' statement was widely condemned . <p> " There was n't even 24 hours of sympathy on the Harvard campus for 1,200 Israelis being murdered , raped , killed , taken hostage , " Ackman , who is Jewish , recalled to the Globe . <p> Maya Bodnick , a Jewish undergrad , pushed back on the suggestion that the attack was somehow bound to happen because of Israel 's treatment of Palestinians . " This was a massacre ! It was n't inevitable , " she said to her boyfriend , who was Muslim , as she later recounted in a Globe essay . Nothing justifies " slaughtering over a thousand Jews . " <p> Two days later , Gay and other leaders put out a statement on " the war in Israel and Gaza now underway , " only to see it criticized by some for being too even-handed and late . She issued her own statement a day later , condemning the " terrorist atrocities perpetrated by Hamas . " But by then the damage was done . <p> Ackman called on Harvard to release names of those in the student groups , saying future employers had a right to know the type of people they were thinking of hiring . <p> A few days after the Oct. 7 attack , Barron saw a truck parked in Harvard Square . It displayed huge photos of students allegedly aligned with the group statement , labeling them " Harvard 's Leading Antisemites . " The conservative group behind the truck , Accuracy in Media , was also setting up websites in the names of protesters that included their personal information , exposing them to threats . <p> The doxxing of students stunned Barron . It made her want to know more about what those students thought and how they felt . She plunged into deeper reading about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict , but from a perspective she had never been taught growing up in America , the Palestinian point of view . <p> Reports of antisemitic comments and shunning on campus were alarming Jewish communities at Harvard , Columbia , Massachusetts Institute of Technology , and other schools . On Sidechat , a social media service popular on campuses , anonymous posts reportedly included anti-Israeli messages like " I proudly accept the label of terrorist . " The university increased security at the Harvard Hillel building . <p> Controversy erupted again on Oct. 18 , when an Israeli-American student on the Harvard Business School lawn began using his phone to film protesters at an anti-Israel " die-in . " Some worried his images would end up on doxxing trucks , which had appeared in Cambridge the week before . <p> During an Oct. 18 , 2023 , pro-Palestinian demonstration at Harvard Business School , protesters try to block a man from filming on his phone . ( Pat Greenhouse/Globe Staff ) <p> Protesters surrounded him , trying to block him from filming with their keffiyehs , and there was some jostling and physical contact . When Garber , Harvard 's provost , reviewed video of the incident , he seemed uncertain aboutwho was most responsible for escalating it . The student " was technically within his rights " to film there , and yet the " way he was taking videos appears provocative , " according to a text he sent to a colleague , which was obtained by a congressional committee . <p> The interaction was complex , but social media rarely allows for nuance . Video clips circulated widely online , some seemingly edited for maximum outrage , with such captions as : " Harvard students attacking a Jewish student on campus during an anti-Israel protest . " <p> That characterization took hold , with USSenator Mitt Romney and four other business school alumni describing it as the " violent assault of an Israeli student " in an open letter to Harvard . <h> Stefanik vs . Gay <p> Some Republicans in Congress demanded an explanation for what was happening on college campuses . For a House Education Committee hearing on Dec. 5 , 2023 , they summoned three presidents to Washington to testify : Gay of Harvard , Liz Magill of the University of Pennsylvania , and Sally Kornbluth of MIT . <p> The topic of the day was allegations of rising antisemitism , but lawmakers also took the opportunity to attack elite universities more broadly on topics including DEI . <p> " What I am describing is a grave danger inherent in assenting to the race-based ideology of the radical left , " said committee chair Virginia Foxx , a North Carolina Republican , addressing the university leaders . " Institutional antisemitism and hate are among the poisoned fruits of your institutions ' cultures . " <p> Gay had been thoroughly prepared by lawyers , including in the language of Harvard 's new " Non-Discrimination and Anti-Bullying " policy . Finalized just three months earlier , it sought to clarify a major legal issue for volatile campuses : When exactly do officials punish a student to stop offensive speech ? <p> Harvard had developed a nuanced answer . Offensive statements broadcast by a student to a general audience may be abhorrent but were likely protected as free speech . However , a student whose words targeted an individual could be sanctioned , if the comments were " so severe or pervasive , and objectively offensive " that they interfered with the other student 's educational experience . <p> Claudine Gay , president of Harvard University , testified before the House Education and Workforce Committee on Dec. 5 , 2023 , during a hearing to investigate antisemitism on college campuses . ( Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images ) <p> Representative Elise Stefanik , a New York Republican and a graduate of Harvard , aggressively questioned the college presidents . ( Mark Schiefelbein/Associated Press ) <p> " Targeted as an individual , targeted as -- at an individual , severe , pervasive . " <p> Gay was hewing closely to the language of Harvard 's new policy . Stefanik asked the question two more times , and got similar answers . <p> " It does not ' depend on the context , ' " Stefanik eventually snapped . " And this is why you should resign . These are unacceptable answers across the board . " <p> Clips went viral -- though they rarely seemed to include extensive remarks from Gay that " antisemitism has no place at Harvard . " Back on campus , as criticism mounted , she apologized for the legalistic tone of remarks . A billboard truck showed up in Cambridge with a two-word message : " Fire Gay . " <p> Within a week , conservative writer Rufo and a colleague published a piece accusing Gay of plagiarizing parts of her 1997 doctoral thesis and other academic work . Rufo later said his post attracted more than 100 million impressions on Twitter , while saying it was part of a coordinated operation . <p> Advertisement <p> The Harvard Corporation initially stood behind Gay . An internal investigation of the plagiarism claims found some inadequate citations , though no research misconduct . By Dec. 27 , the board 's support had dissipated.That day , Pritzker called Gay in Rome , where she was on a long-planned family vacation . By the end of their conversation , Gay said she would resign . Two days into the new year , she did . <p> In the looming war on universities by the political right , Rufo and his allies saw the toppling of Gay as a proven battle plan , he said . He told Politico it showed " How we have to work the media , how we have to exert pressure and how we have to sequence our campaigns in order to be successful . " <h> The encampments <p> Stepping in as interim president , Garber took steps to quiet the critics and calm the campus . He appointed the task forces to investigate antisemitism and Islamophobia on campus . And he adopted an institutional neutrality policy , which sidelined the university from taking standson political matters that did n't directly affect its mission . <p> A period of relative quiet set in , but it did n't last long . On April 24 , 2024 , as the Israel-Hamas war escalated , hundreds of pro-Palestinian students protested in Harvard Yard , calling for the university to divest from Israel . About 50 students set up makeshift tents to form an encampment , which would become a test of the university 's rules for civil protests that had a history of being unevenly enforced . <p> A pro-Palestinian protest encampment in Harvard Yard , seen through a gate , on April 30 , 2024 . ( Andrew Burke-Stevenson for The Boston Globe ) <p> Among the students was Violet Barron . Her readings about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict had profoundly changed her , as it had other students . " We 've established this encampment at Harvard University to protest our administration 's moral and material complicity in the genocide of what has now been over 34,000 Palestinian people in Gaza , " she said in a video posted on YouTube . <p> Barron 's parents , watching from California , worried about her studies , andpotential disciplinary action . But they were also moved by her idealism . " I do n't agree with everything she is saying , " her father , Eric , told the Globe this summer , " but I am proud of her because she ' s trying to make the world a better place . " <p> As 2024 commencement approached , and the encampment stretched toward three weeks , Garber worried they would need to cancel the ceremony . Four years earlier , COVID robbed these students of their in-person high school graduations , and he did n't want them to miss another one . <p> Garber and the protesters eventually reached an agreement on May 14 . Student protesters secured promises for future discussions about Harvard 's endowment and came to believe they would not be sanctioned severely . <p> But the college 's administrative board , chaired by Khurana , did issue discipline . It voted to suspend five undergrads , including Barron , requiring them to leave school for a year , though they would all appeal . About two dozen undergrads were placed on probation . @@132772473 <h> Palestine Action : Prison hunger strikes that shaped history <p> Four Palestine Action members are continuing hunger strikes in the UK , following a protest practice with a long history -- from Ireland and India to South Africa and Guantanamo . <p> A protester holds placard reading ' Palestine Action ban stops Free Speech ' during a demonstration in support of " Defend Our Juries " and their campaign against the ban on Palestine Action , outside Britain 's Ministry of Justice in London on November 20 , 2025 AFP <p> Four members of the advocacy group Palestine Action have pledged this week to continue their hunger strike amid grave medical warnings and the hospitalisations of their fellow protesters . <p> The group 's members are being held in five prisons in the United Kingdom over alleged involvement in break-ins at a facility of the UK 's subsidiary of the Israeli defence firm Elbit Systems in Bristol and a Royal Air Force base in Oxfordshire . They are protesting for better conditions in prison , rights to a fair trial , and for the UK to change a July @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Palestine Action denies charges of " violent disorder " and others against the eight detainees . Relatives and loved ones told Al Jazeera of the members ' deteriorating health amid the hunger strikes , which have led to repeated hospital admissions . Lawyers representing the detainees have revealed plans to sue the government . <p> The case has brought international attention to the UK 's treatment of groups standing in solidarity with Palestinians amid Israel 's genocidal war in Gaza . Thousands of people have rallied in support of Palestine Action every week . <p> Hunger strikes have been used throughout history as an extreme , non-violent way of seeking justice . Their effectiveness often lies in the moral weight they place upon those in power . <p> Historical records trace hunger strikes back to ancient India and Ireland , where people would fast at the doorstep of an offender to publicly shame them . However , they have also proved powerful as political statements in the present day . <p> Advertisement <p> Here are some of the most famous hunger strikes in recent world history : <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Army in the Ardoyne area of north Belfast , September 9 , 2015 Cathal McNaughton/Reuters <h> Irish Republican Movement hunger strikes <p> Some of the most significant hunger strikes in the 20th century occurred during the Irish revolutionary period , or the Troubles . The first wave was the 1920 Cork hunger strike , during the Irish War of Independence . Some 65 people suspected of being Republicans had been held without proper trial proceedings at the Cork County Gaol . <p> They began a hunger strike , demanding their release and asking to be treated as political prisoners rather than criminals . They were joined by Terence MacSwiney , the lord mayor of Cork , whose profile brought significant international attention to the independence cause . The British government attempted to break up the movement by transferring the prisoners to other locations , but their fasts continued . At least three prisoners died , including MacSwiney , after 74 days . <p> Later on , towards the end of the conflict and the signing of the Good Friday Agreement , imprisoned Irish Republicans protested against their internment and the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rights : the right to wear civilian clothes , or to not be forced into labour . <p> They began the " dirty protest " in 1980 , refusing to have a bath and covering walls in excrement . In 1981 , scores of people refused to eat . The most prominent among them was Bobby Sands , an IRA member who was elected as a representative to the British Parliament while he was still in jail . Sands eventually starved to death , along with nine others , during that period , leading to widespread criticism of the Margaret Thatcher administration . <h> Gandhi and the Indian independence struggle <p> India 's Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi , who was later popularly known as Mahatma Gandhi , used hunger strikes as a tool of protest against the British colonial rulers several times . His fasts , referred to as Satyagraha , meaning holding on to truth in Hindi , were considered by the politician and activist not only as a political act but also a spiritual one . <p> Gandhi 's strikes sometimes lasted for days or weeks , during which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . They achieved mixed results -- sometimes , the British policy changed , but at other times , there were no improvements . Gandhi , however , philosophised in his many writings that the act was not a coercive one for him , but rather an attempt at personal atonement and to educate the public . <p> Advertisement <p> One of Gandhi 's most significant hunger strikes was in February 1943 , after British authorities placed him under house arrest in Pune for starting the Quit India Movement back in August 1942 . Gandhi protested against the mass arrests of Congress leaders and demanded the release of prisoners by refusing food for 21 days . It intensified public support for independence and prompted unrest around the country , as workers stayed away from work and people poured out into the streets in protest . <p> Another popular figure who used hunger strikes to protest against British rule in colonial India was Jatindra Nath Das , better known as Jatin Das . A member of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association , Das refused food while in detention for 63 days starting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of political prisoners . His third comedy special on Netflix , " Mo Amer : Wild World , " premiered in October . <p> Narratively , the second season ends before the Hamas attack in Israel on Oct. 7 , 2023 , but the series itself does n't shy away from addressing Israeli-Palestinian relations , the ongoing conflict in Gaza or what it 's like for asylum seekers detained in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centers . <p> In addition to " Mo , " shows like " Muslim Matchmaker , " hosted by matchmakers Hoda Abrahim and Yasmin Elhady , connect Muslim Americans from around the country with the goal of finding a spouse . <p> The animated series , " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , who worked with Amer to create " Mo , " and Pam Brady , follows an Egyptian American Muslim family navigating life in New Jersey after the 9/11 terrorists attack in New York . <p> Current events have an influence <p> The key to understanding the ways in which Arab or Muslim Americans have been represented on screen is to be aware of the " historical , political , cultural and social contexts " in which the content was created , said Sahar Mohamed Khamis , a University of Maryland professor who studies Arab and Muslim representation in media . <p> After the 9/11 attacks , Arabs and Muslims became the villains in many American films and TV shows . The ethnic background of Arabs and the religion of Islam were portrayed as synonymous , too , Khamis said . The villain , Khamis said , is often a man with brown skin with an Arab-sounding name . <p> A show like " Muslim Matchmaker " flips this narrative on its head , Elhady said , by showing the ethnic diversity of Muslim Americans . <p> " It 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Americans , " said Elhady , who is Egyptian and Libyan American , " but also as people that live in different places and have kind of sometimes dual realities and a foot in the East and a foot in the West and the reality of really negotiating that context . " <p> Before 9/11 , people living in the Middle East were often portrayed to Western audiences as exotic beings , living in tents in the desert and riding camels . Women often had little to no agency in these media depictions and were " confined to the harem " -- a secluded location for women in a traditional Muslim home . <p> This idea , Khamis said , harkens back to the term " orientalism , " which Palestinian American academic , political activist and literary critic Edward Said coined in his 1978 book of the same name . <p> Khamis said , pointing to countries like Britain and France , the portrayal in media of people from the region was " created and manufactured , not by the people themselves , but through the gaze of an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , were the colonial/imperialist powers that were actually controlling these lands for long periods of time . " <p> Among those who study the ways Arabs have been depicted on Western television , a common critique is that the characters are " bombers , billionaires or belly dancers , " she said . <p> The limits of representation <p> Sanaz Alesafar , executive director of Storyline Partners and an Iranian American , said she has seen some " wins " with regard to Arab representation in Hollywood , noting the success of " Mo , " " Muslim Matchmaker " and " #1 Happy Family USA . " Storyline Partners helps writers , showrunners , executives and creators check the historical and cultural backgrounds of their characters and narratives to assure they 're represented fairly and that one creator 's ideas do n't infringe upon another 's . <p> Alesafar argues there is still a need for diverse stories told about people living in the Middle East and the English-speaking diaspora , written and produced by people from those backgrounds . <p> " In the popular imagination and popular culture @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " she said . " Yes , we 're having these wins and these are incredible , but that decision-making and centers of power still are relegating us to these tropes and these stereotypes . " <p> Deana Nassar , an Egyptian American who is head of creative talent at film production company Alamiya Filmed Entertainment , said it 's important for her children to see themselves reflected on screen " for their own self image . " Nassar said she would like to see a diverse group of people in decision-making roles in Hollywood . Without that , it 's " a clear indication that representation is just not going to get us all the way there , " she said . <p> Representation can impact audiences ' opinions on public policy , too , according to a recent study by the Institute for Social Policy and Understanding . Results showed that the participants who witnessed positive representation of Muslims were less likely to support anti-democratic and anti-Muslim policies compared to those who viewed negative representations . <p> For Amer , limitations to representation come from the decision-makers who @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ success of shows like his and others are a " start , " but he wants to see more industry recognition for his work and the work of others like him . <p> " That 's the thing , like just keep writing , that 's all it 's about , " he said . " Just keep creating and keep making and thankfully I have a really deep well for that , so I 'm very excited about the next things , " he said . <p> <p> Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP 's collaboration with The Conversation US , with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc . India , for example , banned the app in 2020 , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ social media this month . <p> Every year , NPR interviews TikTok creators from around the world , exploring the trends , subcultures and stories that drive culture and social change in the Global South . This year , we interviewed creators from Brazil , Gaza , Kenya and Tanzania . The four creators each have amassed millions of views , but they also contributed to a much bigger story : one of hope , advocacy and connection . <h> A different way to play with a soccer ball <p> Becoming a professional soccer player was always Arthur Marques ' ( @arthurzinnv ) goal . <p> " In Brazil , being a professional soccer player is everyone 's dream as a kid , " Marques says through an interpreter . <p> The 20-year-old TikToker sort of made that dream come true . <p> Yes , he plays soccer for a living . But it 's soccer with a twist . <p> It 's called altinha , Portuguese for " a little higher . " Players stand in a circle and keep a ball in the air for as long as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , heads and even their butts -- anything but their hands . Marques ' record is five minutes . <p> Sounds ... a little short . But it 's not . " That 's a lot of time , " Marques says . " It looks easy , but there are a lot of dynamics at play . It 's almost like boxing nonstop for five minutes . " <p> Locals started playing soccer on Rio de Janeiro 's iconic Copacabana Beach in 1927 . But stray balls soon clashed with sunbathers , and officials tightened rules . By the 1930s , restrictions made it increasingly difficult to play the sport on the beach , and while enforcement waxed and waned over the decades , obstacles persisted . <p> So local soccer lovers invented altinha in the 1960s on Ipanema Beach . It has n't always been welcome on Brazil 's beaches though and was even temporarily banned in 2009 . <p> Sponsor Message <p> As for Marques , his dream of becoming a professional soccer player faded when he realized he did n't have the chops for the elite @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , he started practicing the sport and began posting videos of himself on TikTok a year later . <p> While the game is played across the country , its pulse throbs in Rio . To be closer to the scene , Marques made trips to the city from his hometown , S ? o Gon ? alo , about an hour away across the bay from Rio . Still in school and the son of two street vendors , he could barely afford the commute . <p> " My two siblings and I had some difficult times growing up , but it was never that hard because we had each other , " Marques recalls . <p> As his videos began to take off , Marques committed fully to social media . He says he would sometimes stay up until 4 a.m. to edit videos on his mom 's phone -- which was newer and faster than his phone -- and then head to high school two hours later . <p> Marques is now participating in the growing trend of playingaltinha on the street courts of Rio 's favelas -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Neymar -- one of Brazil 's most celebrated soccer players -- even joined Marques for a round of altinha in an old warehouse this July . <h> Forgotten corners of Africa 's history <p> While driving through the bustling streets of Nairobi , Kenya , Valerie Keter ( @valerieketer ) was intrigued by a billboard . <p> " It was advertising a German language school and written on it was , ' Schule , ' " Keter recalls . ' " <p> That question took Keter down a rabbit hole exploring the history of Swahili -- the most widely spoken language in Kenya -- and presenting her findings on TikTok . <p> " From there , I ended up discovering that actually there are more Swahili words that were borrowed from other languages -- not just German , " Keter explains . <p> This epiphany is one of many that led the 31-year-old to make videos on overlooked corners @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ traditional beaded collars of the Maasai people in southern Kenya as she tells her tales . <p> Her passion for history and storytelling stems from the documentaries she watched with her family during childhood . Trump promised that he could bring peace to Ukraine in a single day . <p> What followed was nearly a year of on-again , off-again negotiations , apportioning of territory , administration infighting and a war still without end .
